strengths: Tackles a novel and interesting minimalist imaging scenario (single flat optic + filterless grayscale sensor at full output resolution) that, to the authors' knowledge, has not been previously solved, and clearly motivates why it is important (compact, light-efficient, high-resolution snapshot HSI).

Technically sound integration of patch-based diffusion with PSF-derived physical guidance to resolve cross-patch ambiguity; the guidance mechanism (least-squares patch rescaling + gradient-based consistency updates) is well-motivated and clearly described with pseudocode.

Strong and fairly comprehensive experimental validation: comparisons against 8 state-of-the-art baselines across three measurement types (filterless, Bayer+optic, Bayer+ideal), consistently favorable results, thorough ablations (patch size, stride, rescaling, guidance iterations), lens design comparison across 8 PSFs, interpretability analysis via saliency maps, cross-dataset generalization to unseen resolutions/datasets without finetuning, and supplementary noise robustness study.

The uncertainty quantification via multiple diffusion samples is a nice byproduct that is empirically validated (Pearson correlation 0.80 with true error), adding practical value beyond point estimates.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed methodological descriptions, model configuration tables, PSF design theory, and stated intent to release code.

The surprising finding that patch sizes as small as the PSF support suffice, and that guidance is what makes this feasible, is a genuinely useful and non-obvious empirical insight for the patch-diffusion inverse-problem community.
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted purely in simulation; no real hardware (metalens + sensor) validation is shown, so it remains unclear how sensitive the method is to real-world PSF calibration errors, fabrication imperfections, or sensor nonlinearities not captured by the simulator.

The comparison baselines (SST, SPECAT, MST, etc.) were designed for CASSI-style coded-aperture compressive sensing with masks, not for this filterless single-optic setting; retraining them with minimal modification may understate their true achievable performance and could be seen as a somewhat unfair comparison, even though the authors are transparent about this.

The method's runtime is dominated by the guidance loop (tens of seconds per image at moderate iteration counts), which may limit practicality for real-time or large-scale deployment despite the parallel patch processing.

Scale ambiguity per patch is corrected via a non-differentiable least-squares step during guidance, which the authors admit introduces "a minor reduction in accuracy" - the impact of this approximation is not deeply quantified beyond one ablation row.

The paper does not discuss how robust the lens designs and reconstruction pipeline would be to practical calibration/alignment errors between an as-fabricated metalens PSF and the simulated PSF used for both training and guidance, which is an important feasibility gap for the stated goal of a new camera class.

The cross-dataset generalization results, while promising, show a noticeable performance drop (e.g., PSNR ~32-33 vs ~34.6 in-distribution) and are only evaluated on a small number of test scenes (5-10), limiting the strength of the generalization claims.

Some presentation aspects (e.g., a single Pearson correlation number for uncertainty calibration, limited quantitative detail on how much saliency maps quantitatively match ground truth PSFs) could be strengthened with additional statistics or calibration curves.

strengths: Addresses a novel and well-motivated problem: reconstructing full hyperspectral images from a single filterless grayscale snapshot captured through a single diffractive lens, a minimalist optical setting that is largely unexplored and could enable simpler, more light-efficient snapshot HSI cameras.

Technically sound and creative solution: a patch-based conditional diffusion model combined with an inference-time guidance mechanism that enforces optical consistency (via the known PSF) across patches, directly addressing the key challenge that PSF support is comparable to patch size (unlike prior patch-diffusion works that only handle compact degradations).

Extensive simulation evaluation on ARAD1K against eight strong state-of-the-art baselines with consistent, sizable margins (PSNR +2.86 dB, lower SAM), plus a UNet-regression ablation isolating that gains come from the patch-diffusion/guidance approach rather than raw capacity.

Thorough ablation studies (patch size, overlapping patches, guidance on/off, rescaling, PSF design comparison across 8 lens types) and an interpretability analysis (saliency maps) showing the model implicitly learns to attend to physically correct PSF-informed input regions.

Strong hardware validation: a fabricated metalens prototype, careful PSF calibration and shift-invariance verification, a practical LoRA-based fine-tuning strategy to bridge sim-to-real gaps, and real tabletop reconstructions with quantitative metrics (PSNR 31.2 dB, SSIM 0.89).

Useful and well-validated uncertainty quantification via multiple diffusion samples, showing strong correlation with reconstruction error both in simulation (Pearson 0.80) and on real data (0.69), including per-channel analysis.

Demonstrates generalizability of the guided patch-diffusion framework beyond the filterless setting (cross-dataset generalization to ICVL/Harvard/CAVE, and application to CASSI where uncertainty-based pixel filtering further improves metrics), and includes an insightful ablation disentangling the contribution of the filterless optic vs. Bayer color filters.
High reproducibility: detailed architecture, training, algorithmic pseudocode, and calibration procedures are provided in a substantial supplementary section.

Honest and specific discussion of limitations (homogeneous-region failure mode quantified with a controlled checkerboard experiment; patch independence causing uneven quality across a scene) rather than generic boilerplate.
weaknesses: Reconstruction is computationally expensive (up to 52 minutes per scene for high-resolution real captures), which the paper acknowledges but only partially mitigates (e.g., iteration scheduling), limiting near-term practicality despite fast capture.

Real-world experimental validation is based on a single fabricated metalens design (R1) and a modest set of 15 tabletop scenes (8 held out for test), which constrains the generality of the hardware demonstration; broader real-world validation (more lenses, more diverse/natural scenes, varying depths) would strengthen the claims.

Because no prior method is designed specifically for this filterless single-optic setting, baseline comparisons rely on adapting models built for different (better-conditioned) tasks; while this is handled transparently, it leaves some uncertainty about whether baselines are optimally tuned for this scenario.

The patch-independence design fundamentally limits propagation of global context beyond shared boundaries, causing observed uneven reconstruction quality within a scene (e.g., partial flower regions in Fig. 5), which is an acknowledged but still consequential limitation for practical deployment.

The homogeneous-region failure mode is an inherent constraint of encoding spectral information purely via local spatial chromatic blur, restricting applicability to textured scenes; this fundamentally limits the class of scenes for which the method is reliable.

strengths: Introduces and rigorously studies a genuinely novel and challenging sensing scenario: reconstructing a 31-channel HSI from a single filterless panchromatic snapshot encoded only by a diffractive lens's chromatic PSF, which is more ill-posed than prior CASSI/CFA-based snapshot HSI settings and is a meaningful new point in the optics/computation trade-off space.

The technical approach (patch-based conditional diffusion with PSF-based cross-patch guidance, per-patch scale recovery via least squares, and stitching) is well-motivated by the specific difficulty that the PSF support is comparable to the patch size, and the paper clearly explains why naive patch diffusion fails without guidance.

Very thorough empirical validation: extensive ablations (patch size, overlapping vs. non-overlapping patches, guidance iterations, PSF/lens designs, noise robustness, LoRA finetuning), cross-dataset generalization (ICVL, Harvard, CAVE), and even generalization to an unrelated encoding (CASSI) where the method achieves state-of-the-art PSNR/SSIM.

Goes beyond simulation to build and calibrate an actual fabricated metalens prototype, capture real tabletop scenes with a reference hyperspectral camera, and demonstrate a working (if imperfect) real system, which is uncommon and valuable for a computational imaging paper.

The diffusion formulation naturally yields well-calibrated per-pixel uncertainty estimates (Pearson correlation 0.80 in simulation, 0.69 experimentally, and consistently high per-channel), which is a useful and rarely provided feature in this literature and is validated across simulation, experiment, and even the CASSI benchmark.

Saliency-map analysis provides an interpretable link between the learned model behavior and the physical PSF, strengthening the scientific narrative that local optical cues (not learned semantic priors) drive the reconstruction, which is further supported by the metameric-scene discrimination test.
weaknesses: The claimed practical benefit (a truly filterless, minimalist snapshot system) is partly undercut by the reconstruction cost: guidance requires up to 52 minutes per scene on a modern GPU for high-resolution data, and even the ARAD1K setting takes ~22s/scene; this is a substantial deployment limitation that is only partially mitigated by proposed speedups.

The patch-based design has an admitted fundamental failure mode on spatially homogeneous regions (where little/no spectral information is encoded), which is common in many real-world images (e.g., sky, walls, uniform backgrounds); the checkerboard experiment quantifies this but doesn't resolve it, meaning practical applicability to generic natural scenes may be more limited than the curated, texture-rich test scenes suggest.

Because patches are only coupled via boundary-consistency guidance rather than shared global context, reconstruction quality can be visibly uneven within a single image (e.g., the red-flower example), and the paper acknowledges no principled fix beyond suggesting future full-image conditioning.

The real-hardware validation, while a definite strength, is based on a small set of 15 tabletop scenes (6 for LoRA finetuning, 8 for testing) with a specific object/material distribution, band-pass filtering at 450-700nm, and homography-based (imprecise) registration to a reference camera; the extent to which conclusions generalize to more complex, larger-scale, or outdoor scenes is untested.

The real system's "filterless" claim is complicated by the fact that a physical 450-700nm band-pass filter is still used at the aperture in the prototype, and the sim-to-real gap requires LoRA finetuning on paired captures from a second, expensive multi-shot hyperspectral reference camera, which adds practical overhead and could be seen as inconsistent with a fully minimalist imaging pipeline.

Baseline comparisons, although reasonably handled (retrained from scratch with adapted forward operators), are against methods originally designed for better-conditioned snapshot problems (CASSI, Bayer-CFA), so the large performance gap partly reflects the artificially harder task rather than a fully apples-to-apples comparison; no prior method specifically targets this exact setting, limiting the strength of the comparative claims.

Training data are limited to ARAD1K (900/50 split, 950 total HSIs), which is small for a generative model; although cross-dataset generalization results are reported, the diffusion model's robustness to substantially different scene statistics or lighting conditions beyond the tested datasets remains unverified.

strengths: Tackles a genuinely novel and severely ill-posed problem: reconstructing full hyperspectral images from a single filterless panchromatic snapshot with only chromatic-aberration cues, going beyond prior filter-array or multi-optic systems.

The core technical contribution—patch-based conditional diffusion with cross-patch PSF-consistency guidance during sampling—is well-motivated and cleanly formulated (scale ambiguity resolution via least-squares closed-form patch rescaling, gradient-based consistency guidance), and is shown to be essential via convincing ablations (Table 2, Fig. 6a) rather than just increased model capacity (UNet-Regress baseline).

Strong and extensive empirical validation: simulation benchmarks against 8 SOTA baselines with clear margins (2.86 dB PSNR gain), cross-dataset generalization to ICVL/Harvard/CAVE without finetuning, a real fabricated metalens prototype with full calibration pipeline, and even a demonstration of applicability to an unrelated system (CASSI) showing the guidance framework generalizes beyond the primary filterless setting.

The per-pixel uncertainty quantification from multiple diffusion samples is a valuable byproduct, empirically validated with strong Pearson correlations to true error in both simulation (0.80) and real experiments (0.69), and shown useful for selecting/pruning unreliable pixels (CASSI truncation experiment).

Thorough and honest supplementary material covering PSF designs, fabrication, calibration, noise robustness, interpretability (saliency maps matching PSF structure), and failure-mode analysis (homogeneous regions), which strengthens reproducibility and scientific rigor.
Physically grounded and interpretable analysis of PSF/lens design trade-offs (Table 3, Fig. 6b) linking optical design choices to reconstruction quality and model behavior.
weaknesses: Baselines are not originally designed for the filterless, large-PSF-support setting; while the authors acknowledge this and add a Bayer-filtered comparison, the primary comparison in Table 1 could be seen as somewhat unfair to methods architected for different (better-conditioned) forward models, slightly limiting how conclusive the head-to-head numbers are.

Reconstruction is computationally expensive (up to 52 minutes/scene for higher-resolution datasets), which the authors note limits applicability to real-time settings; mitigations are proposed but not fully evaluated in the main results.

The method inherently fails on spatially homogeneous regions (acknowledged limitation), and because patches are optimized independently with only boundary-level coupling via guidance, global scene context/semantics cannot propagate, leading to uneven quality within a scene (e.g., large uniform flower regions in Fig. 5).

The experimental prototype relies on a small, imperfectly registered finetuning dataset (6 tabletop scenes with only homography-based alignment and simulated jitter augmentation to compensate for misalignment), which, while reasonably justified, still leaves some uncertainty about how much of the good real-world performance is attributable to this particular calibration/finetuning recipe versus general applicability of the approach.

Real-scene evaluation uses a modest number of test scenes (8), with performance varying substantially across scenes (PSNR 27.5–35.0 dB), and objects are relatively simple/controlled tabletop items rather than natural in-the-wild scenes, so broader external validity is not yet demonstrated.
